doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Language about race and ethnic backgrounds
summary: Thomas amends Rowe's phrasing and says he avoids terms like 'white' that reinforce the idea that race is real.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That’s wonderful to hear. And I have, it’s not exactly the same, but my introduction to the black race was through — you know I grew up in a suburb where there was one African American student who was sort of probably bussed in from inner-city Rochester and of course he was on the basketball team. And it was my introduction to another race of people, was really through Cannonball Adderley and Count Basie. So it’s really great to hear that that music can surround this.

And, if you would allow me, because how we language things, how we describe things, is so important. So I would amend what you just said and say the first time you met a particular ethnic group or cultural group, which some called going back some called Negro Americans, to black Americans, to African Americans, would have been that, like I said, race is not real in that sense. So I don’t believe that there is a black race or a white race. In that same piece that I’m talking about, I have a short portion where I talk about Phil Woods, Paul Desmond and Zoot Sims. And I describe their ethnic background. Part Jewish, part German, and then I have in parenthesis, I say, you know isn’t it like shameful to reduce them to the word “white” where they have this diversity and variety in their backgrounds? You know what I mean? So I don’t use that kind of terminology because I think it reinforces and reinscribes the notion that race is actually real. I don’t buy it.
